title: Paclitaxel + cetuximab every 4 weeks
context_label: Treatment of recurrent or metastatic squamous cell cancer of the head and neck.
indication_text: Treatment of recurrent or metastatic squamous cell cancer of the head and neck.
purpose: Paclitaxel and cetuximab aim to control head and neck cancer that has returned or spread and may help symptoms. Your team explains expected benefit, uncertainty and options in light of your previous treatment.
schedule_summary: Paclitaxel is given on Days 1, 8 and 15, with cetuximab on Days 1 and 15 of each 28-day cycle. There is no scheduled treatment dose on Day 22. Both medicines continue while appropriate, until progression or unacceptable side effects; the protocol does not set a fixed total number of cycles.
administration_text: Cetuximab 500 mg/m² is infused on Days 1 and 15. The initial infusion has a slower maximum rate than later tolerated doses; total time depends on the prescribed dose. Plan for monitoring during and for at least 1 hour after each cetuximab infusion under the current medicine information; confirm the observation plan with your unit. Paclitaxel is usually 80 mg/m² over 1 hour on Days 1, 8 and 15; a consultant may select a 100 mg/m² starting dose for some patients. The actual prescribed dose and premedicines must be confirmed. Day 8 is paclitaxel only.
monitoring_summary: Regular full blood count, kidney and liver tests, with nerve assessment as indicated. The NCCP source does not give one universal testing interval: your unit must specify tests due before each planned visit. Cetuximab product information also requires electrolyte assessment before and periodically during treatment; the team confirms magnesium and other mineral checks.

agents.name: Cetuximab
agents.mechanism: Blocks a growth signal on cells
agents.explanation: Cetuximab attaches to the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) on cells and blocks growth signals. It is combined with chemotherapy in this plan. Healthy skin and nails also depend on this pathway, explaining some of the characteristic rash, dryness and nail problems. This is a different treatment from checkpoint immunotherapy.
agents.watch: Tell staff immediately about itching, flushing, swelling, wheeze or faintness. Report skin infection, eye pain, new breathlessness or marked cramps.
risks: Acne-like rash, dry or cracked skin and nail infections
Low magnesium and other mineral changes

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.mechanism: Disrupts the machinery of cell division
agents.explanation: Paclitaxel stabilises tiny structures called microtubules so cells cannot reorganise them normally to divide. It can also affect blood-cell production, hair follicles and nerves. Tell the team about new tingling or loss of function before another dose; nerve symptoms may build up and can persist.
agents.watch: Report fever, new numbness or weakness, difficulty walking or using your hands, and symptoms during the infusion.
risks: Low blood counts and serious infection
Peripheral nerve damage that may persist
Mouth soreness, bowel changes and fatigue

phases_note: Visits within a cycle are not separate courses. The team records delays, omitted doses and any change of plan. A stamp records completed treatment; it does not authorise the next dose.

day_groups.title: Between visits, with paclitaxel on Day 8

urgent_extra: Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Report breathing difficulty, swelling, faintness, spreading skin infection or painful eyes promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency.

support.title: One written support-medicine plan
support.text: Ask for one list separating prevention medicines, rescue treatment and regular medicines. The schedule must match this treatment and visit. Record what you take and whether it helps; do not double a dose, restart an old prescription or add medicines without checking.

support.title: Preventing sickness
support.text: Each medicine is classified as having a low sickness risk, but symptoms still need an individual plan. Take any prescribed anti-sickness medicine as directed and keep rescue instructions available. Report persistent vomiting or difficulty drinking.

support.title: Cetuximab premedicines and delayed reactions
support.text: An antihistamine and corticosteroid are given before cetuximab to reduce reaction risk. They do not prevent every reaction. Report itching, flushing, swelling, wheeze, dizziness or faintness immediately, including symptoms that start after leaving the unit.

support.title: Skin, nails, eyes and minerals
support.text: Use the skin-care plan from the team, including moisturising and sun protection. Report painful cracks, inflamed nails, pus or spreading redness. Eye pain or visual change needs prompt review. Keep prescribed blood tests for magnesium and other minerals; supplements must follow clinical advice.

support.title: Different premedicines on different visits
support.text: On Days 1 and 15, the steroid and antihistamine for cetuximab also cover these parts of the paclitaxel premedication plan; staff coordinate any additional medicine. Day 8 has a separate paclitaxel-only plan. Later steroid or stomach-receptor-blocker doses may change after tolerance review; do not omit or duplicate medicines yourself.

support.title: Food, fluids and weight
support.text: Tell the team early about reduced intake or weight loss. A dietitian can adapt food texture, supplements and intake goals. Follow an individual fluid plan, especially with kidney or heart problems.

support.title: Mouth and swallowing care
support.text: Follow the mouth-care and pain-relief plan. Report ulcers, thrush or swallowing difficulty early. Ask for a swallowing assessment if food or drinks make you cough or choke; do not assume a general food texture is safe for you.

support.title: Fertility, pregnancy and medicine checks
support.text: Before treatment, discuss fertility, contraception, pregnancy and breastfeeding, including medicine-specific precautions after treatment. Bring all prescription, over-the-counter and herbal medicines to review. The team must check interactions and allergies.

sections.title: Before the first visit
sections.text: Bring your medicines and allergy list, test dates, treatment calendar and actual emergency contacts. Tell the unit about swallowing, hearing, mobility, transport or communication needs.

sections.title: Time in the unit
sections.text: Cetuximab 500 mg/m² is infused on Days 1 and 15. The initial infusion has a slower maximum rate than later tolerated doses; total time depends on the prescribed dose. Plan for monitoring during and for at least 1 hour after each cetuximab infusion under the current medicine information; confirm the observation plan with your unit. Paclitaxel is usually 80 mg/m² over 1 hour on Days 1, 8 and 15; a consultant may select a 100 mg/m² starting dose for some patients. The actual prescribed dose and premedicines must be confirmed. Day 8 is paclitaxel only.

sections.title: Infusion and appointment planning
sections.text: Plan for monitoring during and for at least 1 hour after each cetuximab infusion under the current medicine information; confirm the observation plan with your unit. Day 8 is a shorter paclitaxel-only visit, but checks, preparation and observation still add time. Ask the unit for a realistic arrival and collection plan.

sections.title: Before you leave
sections.text: Check the next treatment and test dates, medicines, pump or line appointments, and who to contact if unwell. Have the team replace and verify every example phone number on the wallet card.

sections.title: Practical support
sections.text: Ask about transport, work, costs, caring responsibilities, an interpreter or a support person. Keep changes to the plan in one record.

chapters.title: Understanding your diagnosis
chapters.intro: Keep the pathology, stage and agreed treatment aim with your records.

items.title: Site and type
items.text: Ask which head or neck site the cancer started in, what the biopsy shows, how far it has spread and how previous treatment affects the options. HPV/p16 tests apply to some tumour sites; they are different from tests of chemotherapy safety.

items.title: Who this plan is for
items.text: Treatment of recurrent or metastatic squamous cell cancer of the head and neck.

items.title: Cancer tests and treatment-safety tests
items.text: Blood counts and organ tests support safe treatment. Scans and examinations assess cancer response. These are separate questions; ask what each planned test is intended to show.

chapters.title: Treatment choices and your priorities
chapters.intro: The consent discussion sets out the personal aim and boundaries.

items.title: Expected benefit and alternatives
items.text: Paclitaxel and cetuximab aim to control head and neck cancer that has returned or spread and may help symptoms. Your team explains expected benefit, uncertainty and options in light of your previous treatment. Ask about reasonable alternatives, including supportive care, and which outcomes matter most to you. A research result cannot predict an individual outcome.

items.title: Changing or stopping treatment
items.text: The team may delay, reduce, omit or stop a medicine after symptoms or test results, a change in benefit or your preference. Record which medicine is affected and what is required before restarting. Do not use an old prescription to restart treatment.

items.title: Other treatment and off-label use
items.text: NCCP identifies this paclitaxel–cetuximab combination and schedule as off-label use; the team must confirm the current licensing position for your actual prescription. Discuss the reasons, evidence, alternatives and uncertainties and document the local consent process. Surgery or radiotherapy may have a separate role, but they are not automatically added to this infusion calendar.

chapters.title: Preparing for your treatment visits
chapters.intro: Use the medicine schedule and logistics pages for the exact visit pattern.

items.title: Your personal checklist
items.text: Check that the treatment name, planned tests, support medicines, transport and urgent contacts are correct. Explain any previous infusion reaction or change in your health before the medicine is prepared.

items.title: When dates change
items.text: A missed or held dose is not a completed dose. Ask for revised blood-test, treatment and pump dates where relevant. The team must clarify whether an omitted weekly dose changes later dates.

items.title: Recording actual treatment
items.text: Record the actual date and medicines received, dose changes, test results and symptoms. The wallet is a brief portable record; the passport holds more detail and does not replace hospital records.

chapters.title: Between visits: symptoms and home medicines
chapters.intro: Symptoms do not follow a guaranteed calendar.

items.title: Responding early
items.text: Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Report breathing difficulty, swelling, faintness, spreading skin infection or painful eyes promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency.

items.title: One usable medicine list
items.text: Keep prevention, rescue and regular medicines separately labelled. Note doses actually taken and whether symptoms improve. Check new prescription, over-the-counter and herbal medicines with the team; do not add or repeat old courses without advice.

items.title: Nerve symptoms and daily function
items.text: Report numbness, tingling, weakness, falls, difficulty doing buttons or changes in walking. Describe what you can no longer do, not just a symptom score. The team may need to change treatment before symptoms worsen.

chapters.title: Mouth, teeth and jaw care
chapters.intro: This is the home for detailed mouth and dental advice.

items.title: Care during chemotherapy
items.text: Use the prescribed gentle oral-care and pain-relief plan. Report ulcers, infection, bleeding or pain that affects eating or drinking. Check with oncology before dental procedures.

items.title: If you have had head and neck radiation
items.text: If you have had head and neck radiation, tell your dentist before invasive treatment. Continue the advised preventive care because effects on saliva, teeth and healing can persist. If you have not had radiation, follow the plan for your current treatment.

chapters.title: Eating, drinking and maintaining strength
chapters.intro: Adapt the plan to what you can manage safely.

items.title: Weight and intake
items.text: Record changes in weight and what limits eating: soreness, taste change, dry mouth, nausea or fatigue may need different help. A dietitian can adapt meals, supplements or feeding support. Do not wait for substantial weight loss to ask for review.

items.title: When fluids or food are not enough
items.text: Contact the team for persistent vomiting, dizziness, much less urine, inability to drink or severe diarrhoea. Fluid goals depend on kidney and heart health. If a feeding tube is needed, ask for training, supplies and a clear problem-contact route.

chapters.title: Swallowing, voice and communication
chapters.intro: Protect safe swallowing and make communication easier.

items.title: When to seek assessment
items.text: Report coughing or choking with food or drinks, a wet voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. Ask for speech and language assessment; use only the textures and exercises recommended for you.

items.title: Communication support
items.text: Tell the team about hearing, speech or voice changes. Request written instructions, an interpreter, communication aids or help involving a support person when useful.

chapters.title: Daily life and personal priorities
chapters.intro: Use the support available around you.

items.title: Activity, rest and practical needs
items.text: Discuss the level of activity you can manage, work, travel and help at home. Ask for assessment if fatigue, pain, weakness or falls disrupt ordinary activities. Bring practical barriers to appointments into the discussion.

items.title: Fertility, intimacy and emotional wellbeing
items.text: Ask about fertility preservation before treatment and specific pregnancy, contraception and breastfeeding precautions. Tell the team about anxiety, body-image, sexual or relationship concerns; support can be tailored to your priorities.

items.title: Smoking and alcohol
items.text: Ask for help with smoking cessation and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth symptoms, medicines and recovery may affect what is appropriate for you.

chapters.title: Recovery, review and longer-term care
chapters.intro: Finishing scheduled doses and recovering are different milestones.

items.title: Symptoms and follow-up
items.text: Continue review of nerve symptoms, skin or nail problems and any abnormal blood or mineral results. The team sets the follow-up tests and disease assessments; this regimen does not mandate a universal post-treatment scan or tumour-marker timetable.

items.title: The next cancer assessment
items.text: Record who arranges examinations, scans and any tumour-specific tests, and who explains the results. A general reference calendar does not set an appointment or mean a scan is overdue.

items.title: Information for other clinicians
items.text: Keep the regimen name, last treatment date, current medicines and unresolved side effects available. Tell future clinicians about any earlier head and neck radiotherapy, platinum-related hearing or kidney problems, and significant infusion reactions.

chapters.title: Your records and additional help
chapters.intro: Essential information should remain usable on paper.

items.title: Passport and treatment card
items.text: Use the passport for the fuller record and the wallet card for the treatment name, contacts and actual completed cycles. Its QR opens this treatment’s information; it does not contain a personal medical record or update paper stamps.

items.title: Complete local contacts
items.text: Every example telephone number must be replaced and checked by the treating service before patient use. Add daytime, out-of-hours and backup contacts and keep them accessible to a support person.

items.title: Reading without a phone
items.text: Read the full handbook in its chapter sequence. The treatment, symptom, contact and practical information does not require scanning a QR or following a hyperlink. Add questions to the passport and bring it to review.

evidence.title: Understanding the evidence
evidence.intro: A phase II study evaluated paclitaxel with cetuximab every 2 weeks after previous platinum chemotherapy and anti-PD-1 treatment.
evidence.population: Patients with recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer previously treated with both platinum and anti-PD-1 therapy.
evidence.comparison: A single treatment group; there was no randomised comparison arm.
evidence.interpretation: This provides evidence of activity in a selected previously treated population. The study used paclitaxel 100 mg/m², whereas this NCCP schedule lists 80 mg/m² with an optional consultant-selected 100 mg/m² start. Its group results cannot be treated as a prediction for the default dose or every patient. Population: Patients with recurrent or metastatic head and neck cancer previously treated with both platinum and anti-PD-1 therapy. Comparison: A single treatment group; there was no randomised comparison arm. Small single-arm study; no proof of superiority over another treatment. Previous treatments and paclitaxel starting dose affect how the findings apply. The combination indication and schedule require off-label discussion under NCCP.
limitations: Small single-arm study; no proof of superiority over another treatment.
Previous treatments and paclitaxel starting dose affect how the findings apply.
The combination indication and schedule require off-label discussion under NCCP.

consent_support: Discuss the individual aim, expected benefit, alternatives and uncertainties; common, serious and lasting effects; infusion reactions and infection; fertility and pregnancy; treatment burden; support medicines and urgent contacts. Discuss the reasons, evidence, alternatives and uncertainties and document the local consent process.

questions.a: Paclitaxel and cetuximab aim to control head and neck cancer that has returned or spread and may help symptoms. Your team explains expected benefit, uncertainty and options in light of your previous treatment. Ask your team to write down the individual aim and explain reasonable alternatives, their burdens and the uncertainties before you decide.

Cetuximab product information also requires electrolyte assessment before and periodically during treatment; the team confirms magnesium and other mineral checks. Confirm the actual dates with your unit.

questions.q: Which symptoms mean I should call immediately?
questions.a: Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, persistent vomiting, diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Report breathing difficulty, swelling, faintness, spreading skin infection or painful eyes promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency. Have the team replace the example numbers with verified daytime, out-of-hours and backup contacts before using the card.

questions.q: How will we decide whether to continue, change or stop?
questions.a: Your team reviews symptoms, test results, treatment benefit and your priorities. Ask when cancer-response assessment is planned and what would lead to a change. A delay or omitted dose must be recorded and does not count as treatment received.

questions.q: What support can help me manage treatment?
questions.a: Ask for a written support-medicine plan and early help with mouth pain, eating, drinking, swallowing, skin or nerve symptoms. Tell the team about travel, work, caring and communication needs. Dietitian, speech and language, nursing and other support can be arranged according to your needs.
